journal.text: Converted the whole dawn hymn, both voices, from VocalTractLab and from Chimera (1,282 credits). Scored all five versions, including the site's Kokoro voice, by whole-hymn transcription: Chimera converted misses 41% (male) and 46% (female) of the hymn's sounds; VTL converted 52% / 64%; the site voice 54% / 59%.

Built a conversion test: 12 dev sentences with 24 χ and 54 s, rendered, converted with the corpus settings, scored before and after. Pilot 2's Chimera loses χ in the converter (58-67% missed after conversion). Going back to the first pilot's brighter single-point χ: 31.7% missed after conversion instead of 36%, s 41% to 19% missed. Held-out raw score unchanged (30.2%). Adopted and committed.

Calibrated the recognizer on real human speech: 1,000 recorded words in 95 languages (UCLA Phonetics Lab Archive) miss 44.9% of their sounds on the whole-transcription measure. Chimera's hymn is 37-43% raw on that measure, so it is at the recognizer's floor there; the per-sound score (30%) still has room.

Your harmonics question: the female voice is too steady (jitter 0.8%) and too clean (harmonics-to-noise 21 dB), and its 4-8 kHz overtones sit 28 dB under the low band (16 dB after conversion). A brighter, rougher source fixes that with no cost raw (dev 29.9% vs 30.0%) but came out 2 points worse after conversion with the same naturalness score (3.32 vs 3.30), so the corpus voice stays as it is. The converter rebuilds the voice quality itself.

h: word-initial h before a vowel is heard 80% of the time after a vowel or a pause, but only 5% of the time after s: the s's release ran 25 ms into the h. Releasing it on time helped h by 2 points and cost s about as much, so it stays off. After conversion the converter hears χ as f, s as ʃ and o as ɔ; a higher s band and a stronger χ improve raw slightly (26.1% on the test set) but converted 33.5%, again worse than the χ fix. Re-converting the χ fix to see whether its 31.7% was a lucky draw: the converter has no seed, so every conversion differs.

The χ fix converted a second time scores 33.5% after conversion, not 31.7%: the first run was a lucky draw. With 12 sentences the voice changer alone moves the result by about 1-2 points, so the bright voice (33.8%) and the louder s and χ (33.5%) are ties with the χ fix, not losses. What these tests reliably catch is a large loss like the old χ (36-36.5% against 32.6% on average). From here, small changes are judged raw on the dev and held-out sets (162 sentences each); conversions are kept for changes that are ready, about 680 credits a test.

Which sounds can the recognizer hear in real people at all? On recorded words from 95 languages it hears palatal stops 5-8% of the time, murmured stops 2 of 9, ə 17%, χ 48%, j 50%, w 57%, h 65%, r 89%. Our j, w, ə and χ are already at or above people's rate; r was far below (61%), so r was next.

The trill: in coda and between vowels the corpus gives r only 28 ms (VocalTractLab's tap), too short for contacts; the engine already borrowed time from the neighbours up to 90 ms. At 110 ms r is missed 27% instead of 44% (held-out), and the whole held-out score goes from 30.2% to 29.7%. Adopted.

Nasals: the velum started opening 70 ms before every nasal, the English habit, so the vowel before it was nasal and heard higher (e as i). Opening 20 ms ahead over 20 ms: held-out 29.3%; syllabic n and m gain most. Adopted. A female-only vowel and tongue-tip retune did nothing measurable; the female voice's 3-point gap is the recognizer's (VocalTractLab's female shows it too).

Labiovelars: the [w] glide after kʷ gʷ cut from 30 to 10 ms; kʷ is still heard as kʷ (or k + w) and the following vowel, usually the e of -kʷe, keeps its own space. Held-out 28.4%. Adopted. Chased what looked like leaky t and d closures; it was my debug readout, not the airway (mouth pressure equals lung pressure and no air flows).

Dark l: l had no tongue-body target at all, so it took whatever its neighbours left. A back, lowered body (a dark, velarized l, the usual syllabic lateral): l missed 8% instead of 48%, syllabic l 35% instead of 59%. Held-out 27.6%. Adopted. The same idea for r made the neighbouring vowels worse, so not kept.

Checkpoint conversion (1,756 credits): the 24 pilot sentences and the whole dawn hymn with tonight's engine. Pilot: raw 27.4% (evening 32.4%), converted 33.8% (evening 35.6%, VTL 56.5%). Hymn converted: male 39% (41%), female 44% (46%). What the converter keeps: χ, s, o, t, d better; what it does not: the trill is much better raw but flattened again after conversion, and m, i, u, w look worse though each has only 14-40 instances. Next: whether the converter wants some vowel nasality to rebuild m and n.

Readiness for the full corpus run: pulled the VTL build's 4,238 clip timings from the desktop (read only) and wrote a full-corpus renderer that also copies each clip's pitch shift (±2 semitones) and accent height (3.6-4.4) from the VTL build, so the new corpus varies its prosody the way the old one did; without that every clip would share one pitch habit. All 4,238 rendered in about 16 minutes with no errors and no length mismatches (10.4 hours of audio).

The corpus QC gate on those renders found a real defect the recognizer had hidden: u was far too quiet, 10-25 dB under the other vowels and often devoiced (2,157 weak-vowel flags). Its tongue body nearly closed on the soft palate (0.01 cm²), turning u into something close to a velar fricative. A less retracted tongue with tighter lip rounding keeps u's low F1 from the lips instead: weak u's 27% → 7%, held-out 27.5% (no accuracy cost). Re-rendering the full corpus with this fix now.

Full corpus re-rendered with the u fix: clips failing the voicing check 616 → 362, more than one weak vowel 1,040 → 540; leaving aside the h and χ brightness floors (meant for restored audio), 3,361 of 4,238 clips pass as raw sources. Most remaining voicing flags are trilled syllabic r̩, which the QC's pitch tracker loses between contacts (it is voiced for most of its length). The hymn's ú in dʰúgh₂ter rose from 14-16 dB under the other vowels to 5-6 dB; converted again (646 credits), it scores a little worse than the night version, but in sounds the fix does not touch (e, w, t), which is the voice changer's own variation. Engine ready for the full run; the renders are on disk (10.4 h, 44.1 kHz, the VTL build's names and lengths).

u, second pass: the first fix had fronted u (male F2 +132 Hz over the reference). A midpoint, tongue slightly back and lips a little tighter, puts the male u within 28 Hz of the reference and keeps it open and voiced; weak u's 10% (27% before tonight). The female u stays about 150 Hz front, because backing it closes the velar passage again in the smaller tract. Held-out 27.0%.

Pilot 4, the readiness test at the final engine (1,110 credits): raw 27.9%, converted 35.0% (pilot 3: 27.4 / 33.8; VTL 56.5). Sentence by sentence the raw renders are nearly identical to pilot 3, yet the converted results swing by 2-4 sounds either way, so the difference is the voice changer's own variation. The male voice converted better (30.0%), the female worse (40.0%), both within that spread.

An open decision for you: the corpus QC gate has brightness floors for h and χ. VTL's raw renders pass them (h median 0.84 of its energy in 2-8 kHz, χ 0.57); Chimera's h is far darker (about 0.2-0.4) because I darkened it earlier to stop the recognizer hearing h as s. A brighter h (breath band to 2 kHz) moves it into the documented range (0.52) with h recognized just as well, but costs 0.4 points on the neighbouring vowels. Converted h is mostly lost either way (VTL's too); your restoration stage re-lays it. I left h as is: accuracy first.

Voice test (5,083 credits): a 25-second passage of 41 real PIE words with every sound at least four times, converted into 15 library voices (Hindi, Marathi, Spanish, Italian, Czech, German, Greek, Croatian; screened from 243 by preview quality) and twice into each current voice. The current voices' two runs differ by 2-7 points, and all candidates fall inside that spread: no voice is measurably more accurate, and none keeps the murmured stops (17-19 of 21 missed everywhere, native Hindi and Marathi voices included). Audio quality differs: Croatian Ivana and Spanish Sandra convert with a much cleaner noise floor (-64 and -62 dB against -46 for W02); Czech Hanka and Greek Jane are dull (8.9 and 12.4 kHz); German Tristan is noisy. Converting each clip twice and keeping the better looked like a 3-point gain, but choosing on half the sounds and scoring the other half shows none: the differences are scattered sound by sound.

Your picks. Male: the 12 male pilot sentences converted into Czech Zazy miss 26.4% of sounds, against 30.0% and 31.2% for our current male voice on the same renders, equal or better on almost every sound (t, j, r most). Female, second pass: 1,001 professional female voices in 40 languages screened for a full low end and real top-end detail (your 'thin' turned out to be a weak low end or a dull top in the converted audio); 8 converted. After conversion most lose their top above 11-12 kHz; Marathi Purna (fuller and a little more detailed than W02, same bandwidth) and Spanish Valeria (cleaner, slightly duller top) are the two to listen to. Accuracy does not separate them from W02.
